name: Godwin's Law
statement: As an online discussion grows longer, the probability of a comparison to Hitler or the Nazis approaches one.
meaning: The longer any heated internet argument runs, the more inevitable it becomes that someone will liken an opponent, or their position, to Hitler or the Nazis.
mechanism: Hitler and the Nazis are the culture's most universally available symbol of absolute evil, so as a dispute lengthens and tempers rise, that maximally emphatic comparison is the escalation people reach for. The 'approaches one' is rhetorical, not a measured statistic — the point is that given enough time and heat, the comparison becomes the default rhetorical nuclear option.

examples.text: A Usenet tradition, recorded in the hacker Jargon File, added a rule Godwin never wrote: once someone invokes the Nazis, the thread is over and whoever made the comparison has automatically lost. Godwin himself resists this, saying the law should start a conversation, not end one.

After the 2017 Charlottesville rally, Godwin publicly waved his own law aside: 'By all means, compare these shitheads to the Nazis. Again and again. I'm with you.' Comparing actual swastika-bearing marchers to Nazis, he argued, honours the law's spirit rather than breaking it.

variants.name: Reductio ad Hitlerum
variants.text: The formal fallacy Godwin's Law informally tracks — coined by the philosopher Leo Strauss (1951–53): dismissing a view merely because Hitler is said to have shared it. 'A view is not refuted by the fact that it happens to have been shared by Hitler.'

variants.name: Quirk's exception
variants.text: The recognised corollary that deliberately invoking Godwin's Law to force a thread to end does not count — you cannot win by triggering the law on purpose.

whyItMatters: It is a mirror held up to online argument: a Nazi comparison is usually a sign that a discussion has overheated and reason has left the room. Godwin built it deliberately, as a 'memetic' nudge to make people invoke history mindfully rather than reach for the cheapest possible outrage.

working.lead: Read the comparison as a thermometer
working.text: when a thread reaches for Hitler, it usually signals that the argument has stopped being about the argument; treat it as a cue to cool down or step away.
shouting 'Godwin's Law!' to dismiss a considered historical comparison is its own fallacy; the law targets glib analogies, not apt ones.
if a comparison to the 1930s is genuinely earned, make it with evidence and analysis — that is the discipline Godwin was trying to encourage.

limits: It is an observation and a rhetorical nudge, not a law of nature or a fatalism — Godwin has said it was 'never meant to be predictive.' It does not hold that all Nazi comparisons are fallacious: apt, considered historical analogies are legitimate and sometimes necessary, and Godwin objects only to frivolous, reflexive ones. The most common misuse is citing the law to shut down a well-founded comparison — treating a valid argument as if it were mere hyperbole. The 'whoever mentions the Nazis loses' rule is folk tradition, not part of Godwin's own formulation.
misreadings: It does not say every Nazi comparison is wrong, nor that discussions are doomed — it observes a tendency and gently discourages cheap analogies. Reading it as 'you may never compare anything to the Nazis' inverts its author's intent, who insists that earned comparisons are fair.
origin: Coined by the American attorney Mike Godwin in 1990 on early internet forums, chiefly Usenet. He has described it as a deliberate 'experiment in memetics' — a counter-meme seeded to create a disincentive for the reflexive Hitler comparisons he felt trivialised the Holocaust — and documented the method in a 1994 Wired article, 'Meme, Counter-meme'. The 'loser' corollary was added later by the Usenet community, not by Godwin.

sources.text: Godwin, M. "I created Godwin's Law in 1990, but it wasn't a prediction — it was a warning." R Street Institute. — Godwin's own account of its purpose.
